It asks for something that can fetch weather. We describe that ability with a protocol, from lesson 4.

Now the view model works with any type that meets the protocol. In the real app you give it the real service. In a preview you give it a fake one that answers at once with sample data, with no internet. In a test you give it a fake that fails on purpose, to check your error handling. This is the main practical reason for the whole idea.
Using the view model in a view

If Xcode complains about main-actor isolation in the view's `init` (newer Xcode versions are stricter), mark the view's `init` or the whole view `@MainActor`. The message names the line, and the fix is one word.

With an `@Observable` class, the view keeps it in `@State`, so that SwiftUI creates it once and keeps it alive. For something shared by many screens, such as the logged-in user or app settings, you can put the object in the **environment** with `.environment(settings)` at the top, and read it in any view with `@Environment(Settings.self)`.
The other names you will hear

items: **MVC** (Model View Controller): Apple's original pattern for UIKit. The view controller often grew huge, which gave rise to the joke name *Massive View Controller*. MVVM was partly a reaction to it.
**VIPER** (View, Interactor, Presenter, Entity, Router): splits an app into many small pieces with strict roles. It brings a lot of files, so you see it in some large UIKit teams.
**Clean Architecture**: arranges code in layers, so that business rules do not depend on screens, databases or the network.
**Coordinator pattern**: one object decides which screen comes next, so that screens do not know about each other. Popular in UIKit. SwiftUI's `NavigationStack` covers much of this need.

**Repository pattern**: one type is the single place to get and save a kind of data. The view model asks the repository, and does not care whether the data comes from the network, a file or the database.
**SOLID**: five design habits, such as *one reason to change per type* and *depend on protocols, not on concrete types*. What you did with `WeatherServing` is one of them.

content.text: Do not over-build. A small app with a few screens does not need five layers. For simple screens, `@Query` straight in a view is fine, and Apple's own examples do it. Add a view model when a screen has real logic or needs tests. The skill that interviewers look for is knowing *why* you choose a structure, and not how many layers you can draw.
Common mistakes

items: Creating the service inside the view model, which makes tests need the real network.
Passing the whole view model to every small child view. Pass just the values and closures the child needs.
Making a view model that imports SwiftUI types, such as `Color`, which ties logic to the screen.

content.text: Your task

items: Move the networking logic of `WeatherView` into `WeatherViewModel`.
Add the `WeatherServing` protocol and a `FakeWeatherService`.
Use the fake in a `#Preview` so that it shows a temperature with no internet.
Write down, in your own words, three things MVVM gives you and one case where it would be too much.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: The app works as before, and the preview works without a network.
The view does not contain any call to `URLSession`.
You can explain dependency injection in one sentence, with the weather example.

steps.say: The view shows the state and tells the view model what the user did.
The view model holds the state and the logic, with no SwiftUI controls inside.
It talks to its service only through a protocol, so it does not know which one it has.
The app gives it the real service. Previews and tests give it a fake one.

faqs.q: What is MVVM in SwiftUI?
faqs.a: A way to split an app: the model holds data and rules, the view shows it, and the view model sits between them with the state and logic. It makes logic easy to test without a screen.

faqs.q: What is the difference between @Observable and ObservableObject?
faqs.a: @Observable is the newer macro for iOS 17 and up. Views redraw only for the properties they read. ObservableObject with @Published is the older approach that you will still see in many code bases.

faqs.q: What is dependency injection?
faqs.a: A type receives what it needs from outside instead of creating it. With a protocol, you can inject a real service in the app and a fake one in previews and tests.

quiz.q: In MVVM, what does the view model hold?
options: The state and logic the view needs

quiz.q: What is dependency injection?
options: A type receives what it needs from outside instead of creating it
quiz.explain: With a protocol you can inject a fake in tests and previews.

quiz.q: Which macro, for iOS 17 and up, makes a class observable by SwiftUI views?

notes: MVVM: Model = data, View = screen, ViewModel = state and logic between them.
`@Observable` class (iOS 17+) replaces ObservableObject/@Published. Views redraw only for properties they read.
Mark view models `@MainActor`. `private(set)` lets only the view model change state.
Dependency injection: pass in what a type needs (a protocol), do not create it inside.
Real service in the app, fake in previews and tests.
MVC, VIPER, Clean Architecture, Coordinator, Repository, SOLID: know the names. Do not over-build small apps.

lessons.title: Testing iOS Apps: Swift Testing, XCTest and XCUITest
lessons.metaTitle: Testing iOS Apps: Swift Testing and XCTest
lessons.description: Write unit tests with Swift Testing and XCTest, test a view model with a fake service, automate taps with XCUITest, and learn what Quick and Nimble are.

content.text: A test is a small program that runs your code and checks the result. You write it once, and it checks again every time you change something. Tests do not remove all bugs. They catch the ones that would come back, and they let you change code without fear. Employers value them because they show you can work on code other people depend on.
What kinds of tests there are

items: **Unit tests** check a small piece of logic, such as a validation rule or a view model, with no screen.
**UI tests** drive the real app like a user: launch, tap, type and look at what appears. They are slower, so write fewer of them for the main flows.
**Manual testing** still matters, on real phones, with different text sizes and with no network.

content.text: In Xcode, tick **Include Tests** when you create a project, or add a **Unit Testing Bundle** target to an existing one. You run tests with Command and U, or with the small diamond next to a test. A green mark means it passed.
Swift Testing

**Swift Testing** is Apple's newer test framework, available from Xcode 16. A test is a function with `@Test`. You check values with `#expect`. If an expectation is false, the test fails and the message shows both sides.

items: `@testable import` lets tests see your app's internal code. Use your own app's module name.
`#expect(throws:)` checks that a call throws the error you expect.
`@Test(arguments:)` runs the same test once for each value, which keeps the list of cases in one place.
A test that throws is a failed test, so mark such tests `throws`.

content.text: Testing a view model with a fake
This is where the work of lesson 13 pays off. We give the view model a fake service that fails, and check that the state becomes `failed`.
The test never touches the internet, so it is fast and always gives the same result. That is what you want from a unit test. `Issue.record` fails the test with a message of your choice.
XCTest

**XCTest** is the older framework, and it is still everywhere. Test classes inherit from `XCTestCase`, and every method whose name starts with `test` runs. You check values with functions such as `XCTAssertEqual`. UI tests use XCTest too. Expect to read both styles in jobs, and the same ideas apply.
Comparing decimal numbers needs an *accuracy* value, as above, because decimal arithmetic on computers is not always exact. The same is true in many languages.
XCUITest: testing like a user

Add a **UI Testing Bundle** target. A UI test launches your app in a separate process and finds controls by their label or by an **accessibility identifier**, a name you give to a view so tests, and assistive tools, can find it.

UI tests can be slow and a little fragile, so keep them for your most important paths, such as signing in or adding the main item. For these tests you often want a clean, known state, for example an in-memory database from lesson 12 and a fake service. A common trick is to pass a launch argument that tells the app to use them.
Quick and Nimble, and what to do first

**Quick** and **Nimble** are third-party libraries that offer a more descriptive style of test, `describe` and `it`, which some teams like. You do not need them. Learn Swift Testing and XCTest first, because they come from Apple and every project can use them.
A sensible testing habit

items: Test logic that could go wrong: validation, calculations, view models, parsing JSON.
Do not test that SwiftUI draws a `Text`. That is Apple's job.
Name tests as sentences, such as `rejectsEmptyTitle`. A failure then explains itself.
When you find a bug, write a failing test first, fix the code, and keep the test.

content.text: Your task

items: Add a test target if your project has none. Write the three validation tests above.
Write a test that checks the total of three expenses.
Write the failing-service test for your view model.
Write one UI test that adds an expense. Give the button and fields accessibility identifiers.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: All tests pass with Command and U. Change an expected value on purpose and see one fail with a clear message.
No unit test uses the real network.
You can say when to write a unit test and when a UI test.

steps.say: A test creates your code, such as a view model, with the inputs you choose.
It hands the code a fake service, so nothing real is called and the result is always the same.
The test runs one action and compares the result with what you expect.
Xcode shows green when it matches and a clear message when it does not.

faqs.q: What is the difference between Swift Testing and XCTest?
faqs.a: Swift Testing is Apple's newer framework from Xcode 16, using @Test and #expect. XCTest is the older one with XCTestCase and XCTAssert functions. Both are in use, and UI tests still use XCTest.

faqs.q: What should I unit test in an iOS app?
faqs.a: Logic that can go wrong: validation, calculations, view models and JSON parsing. Do not test that SwiftUI draws basic views.

faqs.q: Why use an accessibility identifier?
faqs.a: It gives a view a stable name so UI tests, and assistive tools, can find it, even if its visible text changes or is translated.

quiz.q: Which Swift Testing macro marks a test function?
Why give a view model a fake service in a unit test?
options: The test is fast and gives the same result every time

quiz.q: What helps a UI test find a button reliably?

notes: Unit test = small check of logic. UI test = drives the real app. Run all with Cmd+U.
Swift Testing (Xcode 16+): `@Test`, `#expect`, `#expect(throws:)`, `@Test(arguments:)`.
XCTest (older, still everywhere): `XCTestCase`, `testSomething()`, `XCTAssertEqual`.
Fake service in a unit test = fast, no network, same result every time.
XCUITest: `XCUIApplication()`, `.launch()`, `app.buttons["id"].tap()`. Give views `.accessibilityIdentifier`.
Test logic that can go wrong. Do not test that SwiftUI draws a Text.

lessons.title: Publish Your iOS App: TestFlight, App Store, CI/CD and Interviews
lessons.metaTitle: Publish an iOS App: TestFlight, App Store
lessons.description: Prepare an app for release, send it to testers with TestFlight, submit it to the App Store, learn what UIKit, Instruments and CI/CD do, and plan a portfolio.

content.text: You now know the language, the screens, the data and the testing. The last step is the one many learners skip: getting the app to other people. This lesson covers the road to the App Store, the tools you will hear about at work, and how to turn this course into something an employer can see. The rules and prices of Apple's programs change, so for each step we tell you what to look for and where, and not a number that may be out of date.
Before you ship

items: **Name, icon and identity.** Choose a name. Add an app icon in `Assets.xcassets`. Check the **bundle identifier**, a unique name such as `com.yourname.expensetracker`.
**Versions.** Each release has a *version* (for example 1.0) and a *build number* that must go up with every upload.
**Quality.** Test on a real device if you can, with different text sizes, Dark Mode, no network, and a small screen.

**Privacy.** If your app collects data, you need a privacy policy at a web address and honest answers in App Store Connect about what you collect. Apple also asks for details about some system features your code or libraries use, so read Apple's current privacy requirements before you submit.
**No hidden secrets.** Remove test keys, passwords and debug screens.

content.text: The Apple Developer Program

To put an app on the App Store, and to use TestFlight with outside testers, you join the **Apple Developer Program**. It has a yearly fee, and you pay Apple. Check Apple's developer website for the current price, the list of countries and what a free account can and cannot do. In Xcode, open **Settings > Accounts**, add your Apple ID, and in your project choose your **Team** under *Signing & Capabilities*. Xcode can manage the signing certificates for you, which removes a lot of the old pain.
TestFlight: beta testing

items: In Xcode choose a generic iOS device as the destination, then **Product > Archive**.
When the archive is ready, open the **Organizer**, choose **Distribute App** and send it to **App Store Connect**.
In **App Store Connect**, Apple's website for your apps, open the app's **TestFlight** tab. Your build appears after Apple has processed it.

Add **internal testers**, people on your own team, who can try the build quickly. For **external testers**, such as friends or a small group, the first build normally goes through a short beta review by Apple, then you can invite people by email or by a public link.
Testers install the free TestFlight app, try your build and send feedback and crash reports.

content.text: The App Store

items: In App Store Connect create the **app record**: name, subtitle, description, keywords, category, support address and privacy policy address.
Add **screenshots** for the device sizes that Apple asks for. Apple lists the sizes in the tool.
Choose the build, answer the age rating and privacy questions, and **submit for review**.

A human and some automated checks review your app against Apple's **App Review Guidelines**. Read them before you start. Many rejections are about incomplete information, crashes or unclear descriptions, and you can fix them and resubmit. Review times vary.

content.text: We cannot promise how long review takes or that an app will be approved. Apple decides, and its rules change. Read the current guidelines on Apple's developer website and keep your first app small and honest.
CI/CD: building automatically
**Continuous integration and delivery** means that a server builds and tests your app every time you push code, and can even upload builds for you. Names you will see in job posts:

items: **Xcode Cloud**: Apple's own service, built into Xcode and App Store Connect. Check Apple's current plans for any free allowance.
**GitHub Actions**: workflows in your repository that can run on macOS machines. Our Git course shows how GitHub works.
**Bitrise** and similar services: hosted build services made for mobile apps.
**Fastlane**: a tool of scripts that automates screenshots, signing, builds and uploads. It often runs inside the services above.

content.text: As a beginner it is enough to set up one workflow that builds the app and runs your tests on every push. That is a strong thing to show.
Instruments and debugging

**Instruments** is a profiler that comes with Xcode. Use it when an app is slow or uses too much memory. The *Time Profiler* shows where the time goes, and *Leaks* shows memory that was never released. Also learn Xcode's **debugger**: set a breakpoint by clicking the line number, run, and look at the values when the code stops. It is faster than printing.
UIKit: the older toolkit you will still meet

Many established companies have apps built with **UIKit**, with screens called *view controllers*, often laid out with **Auto Layout** rules or in **Interface Builder** (storyboards). You do not need it to start, but job posts often ask for it. The two toolkits mix. You can show a SwiftUI view inside UIKit with `UIHostingController`, and a UIKit view inside SwiftUI with `UIViewRepresentable`. A good plan is: after this course, build one small app in UIKit so you understand view controllers, the life cycle and table views, which are the ancestors of `List`.
Turn this course into a portfolio

items: **Expense Tracker**: SwiftUI, SwiftData, a chart (Apple's Charts framework), tests. You built the base in this course.
**Weather app**: REST API, Core Location, loading and error states.
**E-commerce app**: list and detail screens, a cart, sign-in. Use a free fake store API or your own server.
**AI chat app**: call your own server that calls a language model, stream the answer into SwiftUI. Never put the model key in the app.
Put each project on GitHub with a clear README, screenshots and notes on what you decided and why. Anything you can put on TestFlight or the App Store is stronger still.

content.text: When you are ready to apply, build your resume with our [resume builder](/app) and check it with the [ATS checker](/features/ats-checker). Practise questions on the [interview questions page](/jobs/interview-questions). Look at the [roadmaps](/roadmaps) for what to add next, and use our [Git and GitHub course](/learn/git-and-github-course) for the version-control habits that every team expects.
What to learn next, in order

items: Keep building: one more app each month, a little bigger each time.
Add what job posts ask for: UIKit basics, Combine or more Swift Concurrency, Core Location and Maps, notifications, StoreKit for in-app purchases.
Learn to read other people's code, and contribute a small fix to an open-source app.
Practise explaining your choices aloud: why a struct, why MVVM, why this data layer.

content.text: The next step on this site is the [Advanced iOS Development course](/learn/advanced-ios-development-course). It covers generics, concurrency in depth, memory, Combine, UIKit, secure networking, SwiftData migrations, StoreKit, modular architecture, CI/CD and senior interview preparation.
No course can promise a job. What helps is steady practice, a few finished and published projects, and being able to explain them. You have the base for all three.
Your task

items: Give your Expense Tracker a name, an icon and a bundle identifier. Write a short privacy note that states what data the app keeps (for example, only on the device).
Join the Apple Developer Program if you want to publish, or skip this step if you only want to learn. Then archive the app and upload it to App Store Connect.
Invite one friend as a TestFlight tester, or install on your own device. Write down two things they found.
Push the project to GitHub with a README and screenshots, and write the three things you would improve next.

faqs.q: Do I need to pay to publish an iOS app?
faqs.a: Yes, publishing on the App Store needs the paid Apple Developer Program. Check Apple's developer website for the current fee and what a free account can do, because they change.

faqs.q: What is TestFlight?
faqs.a: Apple's tool for sending beta builds of your app to testers, who install it through the TestFlight app and send feedback and crash reports.

faqs.q: Do I need to learn UIKit as well as SwiftUI?
faqs.a: Not at the start, but many companies still have UIKit apps, so it is worth learning after SwiftUI. The two can be mixed in one app.
